question:
Patient note:
A 72-year-old man with hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and a mild residual hemiparesis of the left lower extremity following a lacunar infarct thirteen months ago was brought to the emergency department by his daughter late this afternoon because he noticed that his right calf had grown noticeably larger during the preceding twenty-four hours. According to the daughter, the patient contracted a febrile bronchitic illness one week prior and, from Monday through Thursday, declined physical therapy sessions and remained in bed except for assisted transfers to a bedside commode; she estimates he was upright or ambulating less than ten minutes cumulatively on each of those four days. He began to feel better over the weekend, sat in a recliner for meals, and this morning attempted to shuffle down the hallway with his quad-cane when the pant leg felt tight against the mid-calf. He denies stumbling, twisting his knee or ankle, or sustaining direct trauma, insect bite, or animal scratch anywhere on the limb. There has been no flank pain, dysuria, fever recurrence, or chills, and he reports no chest pressure, new cough, dyspnea, palpitations, light-headedness, or syncope. He has never been treated for a clot in his legs or lungs, has not undergone orthopedic or abdominal procedures in the past year, and the only device on the left leg is an articulated ankle–foot orthosis worn intermittently for foot-drop related to the prior stroke; no casts, splints, or walking boots have ever been applied to the right side. Regular medications include lisinopril 20 mg daily, metformin 1000 mg twice daily, low-dose aspirin 81 mg daily, and simvastatin 40 mg nightly; he does not take estrogen products, selective estrogen-receptor modulators, corticosteroids, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, or anticoagulants. He quit cigarette smoking twenty-five years ago after a 15-pack-year history, drinks a glass of red wine with dinner on weekends, and denies illicit drug use. Family history is notable for ischemic heart disease in both parents but lacks venous thromboembolism or known thrombophilia. Upon arrival—before analgesia, intravenous fluids, or antithrombotic therapy—the patient sat in a wheelchair with the right leg elevated on a pillow. Triage vitals were: temperature 36.6 °C, blood pressure 138/76 mm Hg, pulse 88 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98 % on room air. He appeared comfortable, conversed clearly, and could move the paretic left limb only against gravity, whereas the right limb flexed and extended fully on command. Cardiac examination demonstrated a normal S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops; lungs were clear to auscultation bilaterally. The abdomen was soft and nontender with no hepatosplenomegaly. Inspection of the lower extremities revealed symmetric thigh contours and ankle girths, but the mid-posterior compartment of the right calf was conspicuously fuller than its counterpart, and a faint lattice of straight bluish subcutaneous channels became evident after thirty seconds of dependency, emptying promptly with passive elevation. A flexible tape placed exactly 10 cm distal to the tibial tuberosity measured 43.1 cm on the symptomatic side versus 39.0 cm on the contralateral calf, producing a difference of 4.1 cm; mid-thigh circumferences were 54.0 cm right and 53.8 cm left, and ankle circumferences at the malleolar level were 24.2 cm and 24.0 cm, respectively. The overlying skin was smooth, normothermic, and similar in color to the opposite limb without erythema, hyperpigmentation, ulceration, or stasis dermatitis. Capillary refill at all toes was under two seconds, and dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses were 2 + bilaterally. Light-touch sensation remained intact throughout, and motor strength on the right side graded 5/5 at hip, knee, and ankle, whereas the chronically paretic left leg graded 3/5 in the same maneuvers. The examiner palpated joints and muscle bellies without detecting bony tenderness, crepitus, fluctuance, or calf firmness suggestive of compartment syndrome; the popliteal fossa was soft without a palpable mass. Straight-leg raise elicited no radicular pain, and passive dorsiflexion of the right ankle produced only a stretching sensation. No inguinal or popliteal lymphadenopathy was noted. A bedside complete blood count drawn before any medication yielded hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL, leukocytes 6.9 × 10⁹/L, and platelets 261 × 10⁹/L; basic metabolic panel showed sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, creatinine 0.94 mg/dL, and glucose 156 mg/dL. Coagulation studies revealed an international normalized ratio of 1.0 and an activated partial thromboplastin time of 28 seconds. A twelve-lead ECG recorded normal sinus rhythm at 86 beats/min with no ST–T abnormalities, and a portable anteroposterior chest radiograph demonstrated clear lung fields. There was no erysipelas, cellulitis, ruptured Baker cyst, muscle tear, or overt lymphedema on examination that could more convincingly explain the unilateral calf enlargement accompanied by visibly engorged superficial veins in the context of recent prolonged bed rest and baseline left-side weakness, so the emergency team arranged urgent duplex ultrasonography of the entire right lower-extremity venous system while the patient remained hemodynamically stable and alert in the observation bay.

Question: What is the patient's score of Wells' criteria for Deep Vein Thrombosis? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Wells DVT score gives 1 point for each positive clinical criterion and subtracts 2 if an alternative diagnosis is at least as likely as DVT.
- Lower-extremity paresis: residual left-leg weakness (3/5) = +1. The criterion does not require paresis on the swollen side.
- Recent bed rest for at least 3 days or qualifying major surgery: essentially bedbound for 4 days = +1.
- Calf swelling at least 3 cm greater than the opposite side, measured 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity: 43.1 − 39.0 = 4.1 cm = +1.
- Nonvaricose collateral superficial veins on the symptomatic calf = +1.
- Active cancer, localized deep venous tenderness, entire-leg swelling, unilateral pitting edema, and previous DVT: none documented = 0 each.
- No alternative diagnosis is at least as likely, so no subtraction.
Total = 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4.
Final answer: 4
